strengths: Novel separate clustering of queries and keys that respects attention's asymmetric geometry, with principled mathematical motivation via dual vector spaces and invariance properties
Theoretically grounded approach using cumulant generating functions (CGF) with clear error bounds O(Tr[Cov(q̃,q̃) Cov(k̃,k̃)]) that motivate K-means clustering
Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrating necessity of key components: dipole corrections (+80% error removal early, +15% late) and two-stage mechanism (+128% error without)
Clear algorithmic presentation (Algorithms 1-5) enabling reproducibility and implementation in other frameworks
Realistic microbenchmarks using actual attention patterns from trained models and end-to-end validation on 30M parameter model
Honest discussion of limitations including single model scale, need for hyperparameter tuning, and clear identification of speedup thresholds (4k+ context)
weaknesses: Modest end-to-end speedup (12.2%) with non-zero loss degradation (0.36%); speedup only on single central layer while other 6 layers use short sliding windows, limiting practical applicability

Large approximation errors (11-25% relative squared error) with inadequately explained relationship to training loss degradation; disconnect between substantial forward-pass error and small loss impact not analyzed
Validation limited to single model scale (30M parameters) on single task (language modeling); no larger models or downstream task evaluation to demonstrate broad applicability
Method only outperforms Flash Attention at 4k+ context lengths; slower at shorter contexts common in current practice, limiting utility
No empirical comparison to other efficient attention methods (Performer, Luna, Linformer) mentioned in related work; only compared against Flash Attention

Hyperparameter sensitivity without principled selection guidance: uses only 1 K-means iteration for speed while acknowledging accuracy sacrifice; implementation specifically tuned for C=64, D=64 square matrices; no principled guidance for new configurations
Theoretical-practice gap: separate clustering motivated via basis invariance in dual space, but implementation uses Euclidean metric 'for simplicity,' weakening theoretical grounding

Incomplete backward pass analysis: gradient flow properties and training dynamics not systematically studied despite acknowledged early-training sensitivity (Table 3 shows 80% error variation at 200M tokens)
Causal attention implementation via hierarchical block decomposition is relatively straightforward without detailed error analysis of log-sum-exp merging in Eq. 8
Isolated attention layer benchmarks show 20-30× speedup at 64k context, but this is not validated in actual pretraining; end-to-end results only go to 16k context

strengths: Sound mathematical framework using cumulant generating functions with rigorous error analysis
Novel separate query/key clustering based on attention's mathematical invariance properties, well-motivated and distinct from prior work
Comprehensive experimental validation including detailed ablations (Table 3) demonstrating each component's contribution
Practical speedups demonstrated (3× at 8k context, 20-30× at 64k) with low approximation error (11-25%)
Clear algorithmic presentation with well-structured pseudocode and intuitive visualizations (Figures 1-2)
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging scale constraints and future work directions
Two-stage mechanism elegantly preserves more Taylor expansion terms than single-stage alternatives
weaknesses: Limited experimental scale: all validation on single A100 with 30M parameters; no scaling experiments to larger models where benefits could be more substantial
Modest end-to-end speedup (12.2%) constrained by experimental design: only one of seven layers uses full 16k context, others use 256-token sliding window
Incomplete practical analysis: uses only 1-5 K-means iterations without rigorous justification; trade-off between clustering cost and approximation quality underexplored
Backward pass error not theoretically characterized; relies entirely on empirical validation despite theoretical focus on forward pass
No downstream task evaluation; experiments limited to next-token prediction on Project Gutenberg; generalization unclear
Missing experimental comparisons with other approximate methods (Performer, Linformer) in end-to-end training despite detailed related work discussion
Head dimension fixed at D=64 with D<64 explicitly excluded, limiting applicability claims; results at 4k context relegated to appendix
'Partially specialized dipoles' represents significant practical compromise reducing accuracy from O(qq̃k̃²) but justification is primarily engineering-driven rather than principled

strengths: Novel and well-motivated separate clustering of queries and keys with theoretical justification based on dual vector spaces, empirically validated with 4-5.6× error reduction in monopole component
Comprehensive multi-scale experimental validation from microbenchmarks to end-to-end 1B-parameter pretraining with power-law scaling fits (R²>0.999) matching exact attention
Practical 36% wall-clock speedup on 64k-context pretraining while matching baseline quality, with drop-in compatibility for existing pretrained models (Llama) without retraining
Thorough ablation studies isolating query clustering benefits (9× effective cluster count advantage) and distinguishing monopole vs retrieval contributions
Excellent reproducibility support with detailed algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameter specifications, clustering implementation, and training configurations enabling reproduction
Demonstrates models learn long-range dependencies even in approximated regions with context utilization analysis showing losses decrease beyond approximation threshold
Generalization validated on existing 8B and 1B parameter Llama models with cumulative mean loss closely tracking exact attention across 8k-64k contexts
weaknesses: Limited primary experiments to head dimension 64 with head dimension 128 only validated at 185M scale; inconsistency weakens generalizability to modern models using dimension 128
Largest-scale experiments at 1B parameters while current foundation models are 70B+; scaling properties to larger models entirely speculative and unvalidated
Context length fixed at 64k with no actual validation beyond this despite appendix F.5 claiming speedups improve at longer contexts; block diagonal cost remains O(N²/S)
Core approximation validity rests on empirical observation that q̃·k̃ cross-terms are negligible, lacking theoretical justification or convergence bounds for when/where approximation fails
Adaptation gap at 1B scale (1.2% degradation with exact attention) not fully explained; fine-tuning remedy suggests systematic biases in approximation but mechanics unexplored
Pallas kernels explicitly acknowledged as not highly optimized with authors stating substantially larger speedups achievable; 36% speedup may be conservative and implementation-dependent
Limited empirical comparison with other efficient attention methods—only MoBA at matched sparsity; no comparisons with Performer, Reformer, Fast Multipole Attention, or other cited baselines

Hyperparameter selection lacks principled approach: balanced assignment cap (4×B/K) empirically chosen; block size shows U-shaped runtime tradeoff requiring careful tuning; no guidance for new architectures
Pretraining-only evaluation with no inference analysis despite inference being actual deployment target; unclear if speedups persist with different workload patterns
Missing statistical significance testing, error bars, and variance analysis across runs; approximation quality depends on K-means initialization but clustering variance not discussed

strengths: Novel and well-motivated separation of query and key clustering with clear mathematical justification (Equation 3); solves a non-obvious problem in attention approximation
Comprehensive experimental validation: rigorous microbenchmarks, extensive ablations (Tables 2-3, 9-15), scaling analysis across 5 model sizes, and generalization to pretrained Llama models
Strong practical results: 36% wall-clock speedup with quality preservation (0.7001 vs 0.7026 baseline loss); achieves <1% approximation error
Drop-in compatibility with existing pretrained models via exponential tilting; critically demonstrated that tilting is essential (Figure 5)
Careful treatment of limitations and comprehensive appendix with implementation details, distributed training considerations, and theoretical derivations
Convincing evidence of long-context utilization during training (Figure 6) and careful analysis of when/where query clustering helps (Tables 2-3)
weaknesses: Limited to 1B parameter scale; unclear if method generalizes to 8B, 70B+ models now standard in practice
Majority of experiments use head dimension 64 rather than standard 128 (Llama); limited validation at head dim 128 (only Table 7 at 185M scale with slight error increase)
Fixed to 64k context with only limited analysis of longer sequences (Table 22); block diagonal O(N²/S) cost may dominate at 256k+ contexts increasingly used in practice
Custom Pallas/CUDA kernels not released; authors acknowledge kernels are 'not highly optimized', limiting reproducibility and suggesting conservative 36% speedup
Adaptation gap at inference: MuSe-trained models lose 1.2% performance when tested with exact attention (0.7108 vs 0.7026), requiring post-hoc fine-tuning on 0.1% of data

Clustering approach lacks principled foundation: single-pass K-means, heuristic 4× size caps, and arbitrary gradient stopping through centroids; no ablation on multi-pass clustering or quality metrics
Limited downstream evaluation (only ARC-Easy, SciQ with noise-level differences) and Llama evaluation only on literary text (PG-19), not representative modern pretraining data
Method complexity with multiple interacting components (clustering, summaries, accumulation, two-level retrieval, local attention); limited comparison with simpler variants
Positioning relative to Hooper et al. (2025a) is incremental (mainly adding query clustering for pretraining); could strengthen novelty narrative

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical foundation: Clear mathematical justification for separate query/key clustering via polynomial expansion (Eq. 3), with rigorous error analysis connecting to K-means clustering objectives

Comprehensive experimental validation: Scaling studies (96M-1B parameters), multiple domains (code and scientific PDFs), microbenchmarks, generalization to pretrained Llama models, and thorough ablations quantifying each component's contribution

Novel technical contributions: Separate query clustering with exponential tilting for exponential-tilt compatibility is original; hierarchical two-stage mechanism with two-level retrieval is well-designed; query clustering provides 3.7-5.6× error reduction for monopole approximation

Practical compatibility and impact: Drop-in compatibility with existing pretrained models without retraining; 36% wall-clock speedup on 64k pretraining; works across multiple domains with maintained training quality

Thorough error analysis and ablations: Appendix B provides rigorous polynomial expansion via cumulant generating functions; comprehensive ablations (Tables 2-3, 13-19) clearly isolate contributions of each component

Good experimental methodology: Custom NIAH evaluation clever and domain-appropriate; multiple evaluation metrics (RSE, correlation, training curves); careful validation of long-context utilization (Figure 6)
weaknesses: Adaptation gap is concerning: MuSe-trained models show 1.2% degradation when evaluated with CUDNN attention (0.7108 vs 0.7026), suggesting approximation alters learning dynamics. While fixable through fine-tuning or non-differentiable aggregation weights, the underlying mechanism is not fully explained

Limited scope of practical improvements: Query clustering and tilting (the novel components) account for only ~17% of runtime (Table 5); retrieval (37%) and block-diagonal (30%) dominate. Query clustering benefit diminishes sharply with retrieval (1.07× vs 3.7-5.6× for monopole-only)

Experimental scope limitations: Single context length (64k) evaluation; most experiments use head dimension 64 with limited validation at 128; single-node 8×A100 experiments only; future work needed for 128k+ context and distributed training

Method complexity with post-hoc fixes: Balanced assignment 4× cap is ad-hoc; non-differentiable aggregation weight trick discovered during review (Table 11); centroid gradient stopping lacks elegant justification; these suggest design not fully principled

Incomplete long-context validation: RULER evaluation performs poorly for both methods (domain shift issues); LongBench results show marginal differences within error bars (Table 10); no evaluation on larger models (70B+)

Reproducibility caveats: Kernels acknowledged as non-optimized research-grade code, not production implementations; Pallas kernels will not match production CUDA performance; effective cluster count analysis uses power-law extrapolation which may be unreliable at distant points
Theory-practice gaps: K-means error analysis uses tilted covariances but implementation uses untilted (footnote 3); adaptation gap suggests theory incompletely captures learning dynamics

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical contribution: Independent query-key clustering is justified by attention's mathematical properties (translation invariance) and polynomial expansion analysis, with 3.7-5.6× error reduction validated empirically

Comprehensive experimental validation: 2× microbenchmark speedup, 36% wall-clock speedup on 1B models at 64k context, consistent scaling laws (loss ∝ params^-0.17) across 96M-1B, rigorous ablations (Table 2, 3, 7)
Practical interchangeability: Drop-in compatibility with existing Llama models without retraining; exponential tilting enables seamless deployment, validated on multiple model sizes

Extensive documentation: Algorithm pseudocode, mathematical error analysis with dipole corrections, detailed clustering procedures, 96M-1B microbenchmarks, and honest limitations discussion including impact statement
Superior approximation quality: 40× lower error than MoBA at matched sparsity (0.006 vs 0.248 relative squared error); matches CUDNN baseline on code and beats on scientific PDFs
weaknesses: Adaptation/interchangeability gap contradicts claims: 1.2% loss degradation (0.7108 vs 0.7026) when MuSe-trained model tested with CUDNN attention on code; requires fine-tuning to remove, undermining 'drop-in compatibility' messaging

Limited experimental scope: Main experiments at 64k context only with speedup at longer contexts marked 'future work'; largest model is 1B (7B+ unexplored); head dimension 128 validation only at 185M scale despite modern models using 128+

Computational speedup only: Figure 3 and Appendix G.5 confirm identical token-level loss trajectories between MuSe and CUDNN, meaning zero sample efficiency gains; all speedup is wall-clock time from faster iteration, not algorithmic improvement

Insufficient long-context validation: Both MuSe and CUDNN score near zero on standard RULER benchmark (Table 31); custom code NIAH is in-domain only; lacks evidence of genuine downstream long-context utilization

Clustering overhead not fully analyzed: Recomputed every forward pass; Table 5 shows 8.4% runtime at current point; claim about 'cannot become a bottleneck' relies on fixed ratio assumption; per-token cost increases 23% from 32k to 128k context (Table 23)
